notes.title: Start here: three sprints on caching, inventory and checkout
notes.body:
Bazaar is a teaching e-commerce monorepo (storefront, admin, API and worker apps over shared packages), built in 15 sprints. Each sprint has a curriculum page in `docs/curriculum/` and usually an ADR in `docs/adr/` that records the decision. This quest covers the three consistency sprints:

1. Sprint 06 with ADR-0006 and `docs/cache-conventions.md`: cache invalidation and stampede protection, code in `packages/cache/src/index.ts`.
2. Sprint 07 with ADR-0007: inventory reservations, code in `apps/api/src/inventory.ts`.
3. Sprint 08 with ADR-0008: checkout and payment idempotency, code in `apps/api/src/checkout.ts` and `apps/api/src/payments.ts`.

Each curriculum page has a **Review before reveal** step: read the naive version and predict how it fails before you read the fix. Do that. The code is written against small *ports* (interfaces) so the logic can be tested without a database; read the class bodies carefully, because the quiz asks what they do in specific situations, and an ADR's one-line summary is not always the whole story.

excerpts.quote: Read the naïve service and red commit, predict the two-success result

readMore.why: What Bazaar is and how the repo is laid out.
The sprint plan behind the curriculum pages.

notes.title: Concept: authorizing stock and money exactly once
notes.body:
Two classic e-commerce failures are *overselling* (two buyers get the last unit) and *double charging* (one checkout is paid twice). Both come from the same root: deciding something from a value you read earlier, while another request is doing the same.

For inventory, read Sprint 07 and ADR-0007, then `apps/api/src/inventory.ts`:

- Compare `NaiveInventoryService.reserve` with the SQL in ADR-0007. Where is the check, and where is the write, in each?
- In `ReservationService`, follow `hold` and `release` line by line, including the `catch` and the `if` on the transition result.

For checkout, read Sprint 08 and ADR-0008, then `apps/api/src/checkout.ts`:

- Compare `NaiveCheckoutService` and `IdempotentCheckoutService`. List every path through `checkout` and what each returns.
- Think through failure points: after the order is created, after the charge, after the response is sent.

Finally read `PaymentWebhookHandler` in `payments.ts` and `signPaymentWebhook` above it: note what is signed and what is checked before the event is processed.

excerpts.quote: A client-generated per-attempt key expresses exactly what “same retry” means

readMore.why: Naive and atomic inventory services, and reservations.
Naive and idempotent checkout services.

notes.title: Concept: freshness, self-healing and stampedes
notes.body:
A cache trades freshness for speed, and it can fail in three ways: it keeps showing old data after a change, it never recovers from a missed update, or many requests miss at once and all hit the database together (a *stampede*).

Sprint 06 and ADR-0006 describe how Bazaar handles each; `docs/cache-conventions.md` gives the key and tag format. Then read `packages/cache/src/index.ts`:

- `ReadThroughCache` and `TaggedCache`: what is stored, and what an invalidation deletes.
- `SingleFlight`: what is kept in `#inFlight`, and when it is removed.
- `ProtectedReadThroughCache`: where single-flight wraps the load.
- `StaleWhileRevalidateCache`: write down what `read` does in each of three cases (fresh, between fresh and stale, past stale or missing) and whether the caller waits.

Also note which parts of the app ADR-0006 says may *not* use catalog caches as truth.

excerpts.quote: TTL-only is simple but knowingly stale.

readMore.why: The cache core: tags, single-flight and SWR.
Key, tag and ownership conventions.

notes.title: Read, check, write is a race
notes.body:
`NaiveInventoryService.reserve` reads a snapshot, checks `snapshot.onHand - snapshot.reserved < quantity`, waits (the injected `concurrencyWindow`), then writes `reserved: snapshot.reserved + quantity`. Two buyers can both read the snapshot with one free unit, both pass the check, and both write `reserved + 1` from the same old value: both get `true`, and the last unit is sold twice.

- *A version conflict*: the port has no version or concurrency token, so the second write simply lands.
- *A row lock*: the service takes no lock between read and write.
- *Redis goes negative*: Redis is not involved in this service at all.

excerpts.quote: await this.inventory.write({ ...snapshot, reserved: snapshot.reserved + quantity });

readMore.why: Sprint 07 objectives, starting with this race.

notes.title: The UPDATE is both the check and the claim
notes.body:
The statement adds to `reserved` only `WHERE ... on_hand - reserved >= $qty`. The database evaluates that condition and performs the update atomically for the row, so when two buyers race for the last unit only one update matches. ADR-0007: "Affected rows determine success." In code, `AtomicInventoryPort.tryReserve` returns that boolean.

- *Redis shows stock*: Redis may cache a hint, but never authorizes a sale.
- *A SELECT first*: a separate read before the update is exactly the naive race.
- *The record saved first*: the reservation record is created after the claim, in `hold`.

excerpts.quote: Affected rows determine success.

readMore.why: The decision section of ADR-0007.

notes.title: Redis informs, the database decides
notes.body:
ADR-0007 makes the database row with on-hand and reserved counts the only inventory truth. Redis "may cache the buyer-facing availability hint but never authorizes a sale", so the storefront can briefly say "in stock" while the reservation itself decides. Sprint 07's debate explains why: Redis counters are fast but drift from the truth.

- *Authoritative counter in Redis*: rejected in the debate as drift-prone truth.
- *A serialized queue*: considered and rejected for its latency; the conditional update is used instead.
- *Reservation records in Redis*: reservations are database records with a short TTL.

excerpts.quote: Redis may cache the buyer-facing availability hint but never authorizes a sale.

readMore.why: The debate captured in Sprint 07.

notes.title: Compensate a claim that cannot be recorded
notes.body:
`hold` first calls `tryReserve`, which claims the stock. It then calls `this.reservations.create(reservation)` inside a `try`. If that throws, the `catch` calls `this.inventory.release(itemId, quantity)` and rethrows. The comment explains why: normally the claim and the record share one transaction, but ports without that facility must compensate at once.

- *Returns undefined, stock held*: `undefined` is returned only when `tryReserve` fails; here the error is rethrown.
- *Retries the save*: there is no retry loop.
- *Returns the reservation anyway*: the `return` comes after the `try/catch` and is never reached when the save throws.

excerpts.quote: await this.inventory.release(itemId, quantity);

readMore.why: Exercise 3: crash between reserve and record creation.

notes.title: Release is guarded by a state transition
notes.body:
`release` calls `this.reservations.transition(reservation.id, "active", "released")` and only `if (changed)` releases the stock. The first call moves the reservation from active to released and frees the quantity. The second call finds it no longer active, `transition` returns false, and nothing else happens. ADR-0007 calls this active-only transitions making release idempotent.

- *Twice the quantity*: the second release of stock never runs.
- *None until TTL*: the first call frees the stock immediately.
- *Only flips the record*: when the transition succeeds, `inventory.release` is called too.

excerpts.quote: if (changed) await this.inventory.release(reservation.inventoryItemId, reservation.quantity);

readMore.why: Short-TTL reservations and idempotent transitions.

notes.title: Events for precision, TTLs for recovery
notes.body:
Invalidation events are precise but can be lost (a crash, a dropped message). With events alone, a lost event leaves an entry stale forever. ADR-0006 therefore keeps a TTL on every entry so it expires and reloads even if no event arrives: "Event-only invalidation risks permanent staleness; TTL-only allows predictable lies."

- *The CDN ignores events*: invalidation must reach every serving layer, CDN included.
- *Single-flight timing*: single-flight collapses concurrent misses; it does not use the TTL.
- *Writes stop publishing invalidations*: the committed write path still invalidates after durable success; the TTL is only the backstop.

excerpts.quote: Event-only invalidation risks permanent staleness; TTL-only

readMore.why: The convention page on events and TTLs.

notes.title: Single-flight shares one promise
notes.body:
`ProtectedReadThroughCache.read` passes `() => this.singleFlight.run(key, load)` to the read-through cache. `SingleFlight.run` returns the existing promise from `#inFlight` when one is stored for the key; otherwise it starts `load()`, stores the promise, and deletes it in `finally`. So concurrent misses for one key share one origin load. Each request still records its own miss in the metrics.

- *A hundred loads*: the miss metric counts requests, not loads.
- *A confirming re-read*: there is no second load; the store is written once per caller.
- *Zero until TTL*: a miss means there is no entry to wait for.

excerpts.quote: if (existing) return existing;

readMore.why: Exercise 2: count origin loads without single-flight.

notes.title: Stale-while-revalidate serves old data quickly
notes.body:
`read` returns `entry.value` immediately while `now < entry.freshUntil`. Between `freshUntil` and `staleUntil` it starts `this.singleFlight.run(key, refresh)` without awaiting it (and swallows its errors), then returns the stale `entry.value`. Only with no entry, or past `staleUntil`, does it `return this.singleFlight.run(key, refresh)`, making the caller wait.

- *Waits for the refresh*: that happens only past the stale window.
- *Returns undefined*: the cache never hands loading back to the caller.
- *An error*: a stale entry inside the window is served normally.

excerpts.quote: void this.singleFlight.run(key, refresh).catch(() => undefined);

readMore.why: Bounded stale data while one refresh runs.

notes.title: The retrier owns the attempt identity
notes.body:
An idempotency key must mean "this is the same attempt again". A cart can legitimately be checked out more than once, for example after a declined card, so deduplicating by cart ID would wrongly merge a new attempt into the old one. Server-generated keys cannot recognise a client retry either. So the browser mints one random key per attempt and reuses it for double-clicks, retries and network recovery.

- *Cart IDs are secret*: the reason is attempt identity, not secrecy.
- *The server cannot store keys*: it stores them, on the order, through `getOrCreate`.
- *Providers reject server keys*: no such rule; the API passes the client key to the provider.

excerpts.quote: cart ID remains a secondary guard, not the key, because one cart may have multiple legitimate attempts.

readMore.why: The debate captured in Sprint 08.

notes.title: Only the creator charges, even after a crash
notes.body:
`IdempotentCheckoutService.checkout` calls `getOrCreate(requestKey, ...)`. On the retry the order exists, so `created` is false, and the method returns `{ order: result.order, replayed: true }` before `payments.charge` is ever reached. If the first request created the order and then died before charging, no request with that key will charge it, and the order stays pending. ADR-0008's "only the creator charges" prevents double charges but leaves this zero-charge gap.

- *Charges now because pending*: the code never looks at the order status.
- *A second order*: `getOrCreate` returns the existing one for the key.
- *A conflict error*: a replay is returned as a normal result, not an error.

excerpts.quote: if (!result.created) return { order: result.order, replayed: true };

readMore.why: The get-or-create decision.

notes.title: Webhook replays are claimed once
notes.body:
`handle` first rejects stale timestamps and bad signatures. A redelivered webhook passes both, because it is the same valid request. It then calls `this.events.claim(event.id)`; the first delivery claimed that id, so this claim returns false and `handle` returns `{ duplicate: true }` without calling `markOrderPaid`.

- *Marks paid again*: `markOrderPaid` is only reached after a successful claim.
- *Invalid signature*: signatures are not single-use; the same body and timestamp verify again.
- *Stale*: staleness is based on the timestamp age (5 minutes), not on earlier deliveries.

excerpts.quote: if (!(await this.events.claim(event.id))) return { duplicate: true };

readMore.why: Exercise 2: replay a webhook 100 times.

notes.title: The signature covers timestamp.body
notes.body:
`signPaymentWebhook` runs SHA-256 HMAC over the string made of the timestamp, a dot and the raw body, and `verifyPaymentWebhook` recomputes it and compares with `timingSafeEqual`. Because the timestamp is inside the signed string, an attacker cannot reuse an old signed body with a fresh timestamp to get past the 5-minute staleness check. ADR-0008's summary says "HMAC over the raw body"; the code signs the timestamp too.

- *The raw body alone*: that is the ADR wording, not the code.
- *Sorted parsed JSON*: the body is signed as raw text, before `JSON.parse`.
- *Event and order ids*: the ids are inside the body; they are not signed separately.

excerpts.quote: createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${timestamp}.${body}`).digest("hex");

readMore.why: The ADR line on webhook verification.

notes.title: Reading the rest of Bazaar's decision records
notes.body:
The newer questions in this quest come from Bazaar's other decision records and two planning documents, not from the three consistency sprints. Read them as a set, in this order:

1. ADR-0001 and ADR-0002: how the buyer and merchant sides are split, and how cache layers are introduced over time.
2. ADR-0003: how sellable variants are modelled.
3. ADR-0004 together with `docs/rendering-strategy.md`: how a route picks a rendering mode, and where server and client components meet.
4. ADR-0005, then ADR-0009: search before and after a dedicated engine.
5. ADR-0010, ADR-0011 and ADR-0012: promotions, order effects and merchant notifications, then currency and locale.
6. `docs/CAPACITY_PLAN.md`: the budgets table and the strategy paragraph above it.

Each ADR is short. For every one, write down three things before moving on: the problem its Context names, the Decision in one sentence of your own, and the cost its Consequences section admits. Several ADRs also record something deliberately deferred or rejected; note those, because a decision is easier to remember next to the alternative it beat.

excerpts.quote: Choose a rendering strategy from business constraints, not framework preference.

readMore.why: The first decision record, and the shape every later ADR follows.
Budgets and triggers for the whole system.

notes.title: Why one Next.js app was the wrong shape
notes.body:
ADR-0001 starts from two audiences with opposite needs: buyers send read-heavy, latency-sensitive traffic and tolerate bounded staleness, while merchants need immediate read-after-write consistency. Serving both from one Next.js application would couple their **rendering mode, scaling, and failure domain**. The Consequences section names the price of splitting: **two deployments**, and deliberate sharing through packages instead of route imports.

- *Auth sessions and two databases*: the apps share domain contracts and the catalog source of truth; there is no second database or sync job.
- *Build cache and two repos*: the ADR says nothing about builds or repositories, only deployments and package sharing.
- *Route handlers and two catalogs*: there is one catalog; route imports are exactly what the split replaces with packages.

excerpts.quote: One Next.js application would couple their rendering mode, scaling, and failure domain
The cost is two deployments and deliberate sharing through packages instead of route imports.

notes.title: Every cached surface names its audience and tolerance
notes.body:
ADR-0002 adds cache layers one measured stage at a time, and alongside that it sets one rule for every surface: it must **name its audience and its staleness tolerance**. The ADR then applies the rule: storefront catalog pages start at 60 seconds, while cart, checkout, inventory mutation and all admin reads tolerate zero.

- *Traffic tier and personalization*: those are columns in `docs/rendering-strategy.md`'s route table, used to choose a rendering mode, not this ADR's rule.
- *Key version prefix and tags*: those are cache-key conventions from a later sprint, not what a surface must declare here.
- *Owning team and runbook*: the ADR names no owner or runbook requirement; layers instead arrive with a baseline and a removal criterion.

excerpts.quote: Every cached surface must name its audience and staleness tolerance.

notes.title: Regenerating the variant matrix is a merge
notes.body:
ADR-0003 stores one `Variant` row per option-value combination and gives each a deterministic, sorted **selection identity**. When options change, regeneration matches existing rows by that identity, so it is a merge: matching variants **keep their IDs, SKUs, prices** and future inventory, new combinations get defaults, and removed combinations that something downstream still references need an explicit merchant decision.

- *Drop and recreate*: that would break every cart line and order line pointing at the old IDs, which is exactly what the merge avoids.
- *Archive and copy forward with new IDs*: matching rows keep their IDs; nothing is copied.
- *IDs kept but SKUs and prices reset*: defaults apply only to new combinations, never to rows that still match.

excerpts.quote: Matrix regeneration is therefore a merge: matching variants preserve IDs, SKUs, prices, and future inventory

notes.title: Why the option matrix is not a JSON blob
notes.body:
Inventory, price, SKU, cart lines and order lines all refer to one exact option combination. ADR-0003's context says a product-JSON matrix is flexible at first but forces **every downstream domain to invent an unstable path into that document**. Explicit rows instead make the variant ID the stable atom of commerce, with a real foreign key from cart, inventory, checkout and orders.

- *JSON indexing*: the ADR does not argue about index support at all.
- *Row size limits*: size is not mentioned; the cost it does accept is more rows and an admin managing a Cartesian product.
- *Renaming options*: nothing in the ADR claims JSON blocks renames.

The lesson generalizes: when several domains point at a thing, give it its own identity rather than a path into someone else's document.

excerpts.quote: forces every downstream domain to invent an unstable path into that document
Variant IDs become the stable atom of commerce.

notes.title: ISR comes with a time bound and an owner
notes.body:
The rendering strategy's decision sequence asks three questions first: can two buyers receive identical HTML (if not, render dynamically), can the value be stale (if not, render dynamically or revalidate against truth), and does the page change only at release time (if so, use SSG). Anything left over uses ISR **with a written time bound and an invalidation owner**: someone must state how old the page may get and who refreshes it when the data changes.

- *Load test and rollback plan*: useful, but not what step 4 attaches to the choice.
- *CDN purge hook and static fallback*: the sequence names neither.
- *Hit-rate target and warming list*: those belong to later cache tuning work, not to choosing ISR.

excerpts.quote: Otherwise use ISR with a written time bound and an invalidation owner.

notes.title: A revalidation window is a maximum expected age
notes.body:
ISR gives static response speed with periodic recomputation, and the strategy document is precise about what its window means: it is a **maximum expected age**, not permission to use cached data for money or stock. Catalog pages may show bounded-stale price and availability, but checkout must re-read authoritative price, discounts and inventory.

- *An exact rebuild schedule*: the window bounds how old a page is expected to get; it does not promise each page is rebuilt on a fixed beat.
- *A freshness promise for checkout*: the opposite; checkout re-reads truth instead of trusting the page.
- *A hard expiry that returns errors*: nothing in the strategy turns an old page into an error; the window describes age, not failure.

excerpts.quote: Its revalidation window is a maximum expected age, not permission to use cached data for money or stock.

notes.title: Keep "use client" at the smallest boundary
notes.body:
In the React Server Components model, a server component's code never ships to the browser. Bazaar's strategy fetches and formats product and collection data in server components so it costs **no client JavaScript**, and places `"use client"` at the **smallest interaction boundary**, such as the Add to cart control. Everything imported below that directive joins the browser bundle, so putting it high would pull the whole product page in.

- *At the page root*: this is the mistake the rule exists to avoid; the whole page would become client code.
- *In the data layer*: fetching and formatting stay on the server.
- *On every component*: that ships everything and gains nothing.

excerpts.quote: so stateful behavior does not pull the whole product page into the browser bundle.

notes.title: Search engines are adopted on measured limits
notes.body:
ADR-0005 keeps catalog search in Postgres (a weighted `tsvector` with a GIN index) until **the 50k-product lab demonstrates a limit**: facet p95 above 150 ms, missing typo tolerance that harms discovery, relevance tuning too costly in SQL, or search load competing with OLTP capacity. Filters stay a closed AST with deterministic fixtures, so any later engine is compared against an honest working baseline.

- *Live catalog passing 50k products*: 50k is the size of the lab dataset, not a production threshold.
- *A vendor benchmark beating Postgres*: the triggers are product limits measured in the lab, not a race on median latency.
- *Merchants asking for synonyms*: feature requests are not on the list.

excerpts.quote: Adopt a dedicated search engine when the 50k-product lab demonstrates one or more:

notes.title: Typesense was adopted for a missing result, not speed
notes.body:
When Sprint 09 reproduced the 50k pure projection, Postgres FTS **stayed under the latency trigger** (78.65 ms p95, below ADR-0005's facet threshold) **but returned zero results for a transposed query**. ADR-0009 is explicit that product requirements, not an unproven speed claim, triggered the move to a Typesense-shaped engine for typo tolerance, faceting, synonyms, pinning and relevance controls.

- *Facet latency crossed the trigger*: it did not; that is the point of quoting 78.65 ms.
- *Search load competing with OLTP*: one of ADR-0005's possible triggers, but not what the projection showed.
- *Relevance tuning costing too much in SQL*: also a listed trigger in principle, but not the observed one.

excerpts.quote: returned zero results for a transposed query; product requirements—not an unproven speed claim—trigger adoption.

notes.title: Reconciliation heals a missed search event
notes.body:
With Typesense, Postgres stays catalog truth and product events upsert the index quickly. Events can be lost, so ADR-0009 adds **periodic reconciliation that compares every derived document and repairs drift**, and makes the drift count observable. The Consequences call this out directly: search becomes eventually consistent, and reconciliation makes missed events self-healing.

- *A TTL on index documents*: the ADR describes no expiry on search documents.
- *A nightly drop-and-rebuild*: reconciliation compares and repairs individual documents; it does not throw the collection away.
- *The merchant resaving the product*: that might publish a new event, but the design does not depend on anyone noticing the drift.

excerpts.quote: periodic reconciliation compares every derived document and repairs drift.
reconciliation makes missed events self-healing.

notes.title: One evaluator, one conditional mutation
notes.body:
ADR-0010 avoids two classic promotion bugs. First, the cart and checkout could disagree about a discount; so **both use the same evaluator**, and checkout reloads the current rules rather than trusting what the cart showed. Second, a usage limit checked and then incremented separately can be raced past; so global and per-customer limits **live in one conditional mutation**, and checkout claims usage atomically.

- *Checkout trusts the cart; nightly limit job*: checkout reloads rules, and a nightly check would let limits be exceeded all day.
- *Separate evaluators; read then write*: two evaluators is the drift the ADR prevents, and read-then-write is the race.
- *Shared evaluator; cache counters*: the first half is right, but limits live in a conditional mutation, not a cache.

excerpts.quote: Global/per-customer limits belong in one conditional mutation.

notes.title: Sprint 10 shipped stacking unguarded on purpose
notes.body:
ADR-0010's final policy is deny-by-default: rules stack only when marked combinable, and totals never drop below zero or configured cost. But Sprint 10 deliberately **kept the unguarded behavior as flaw #5**, so that **Sprint 13's adversarial probe could demonstrate the abuse** before the enforcement was applied. Until then, several eligible codes can produce absurd totals, and the flaw ledger plus a characterization test keep that debt explicit rather than hidden.

- *Deny-by-default from day one*: the status line says enforcement was scheduled for Sprint 13.
- *A two-code cap*: no cap is described.
- *Stacking off for every code*: that is close to the final policy, which is exactly what Sprint 10 postponed.

excerpts.quote: Sprint 10 keeps the unguarded behavior as flaw #5 so Sprint 13's adversarial probe can demonstrate the abuse before applying this enforcement.

notes.title: Refunds are capped by what is still refundable
notes.body:
ADR-0011 bounds every refund by the **unrefunded captured amount**: what was actually captured, minus what has already been refunded. The refund itself is **delegated to an idempotent provider**, so a retried refund request cannot pay out twice. The code follows the same rule: `apps/api/src/refunds.ts` rejects an amount above paid minus already-refunded.

- *The original order total*: two partial refunds could then exceed what was captured, and the ADR does not route refunds through a manual approval.
- *The current catalog price*: prices change; the bound is about money captured, not today's price.
- *The amount on hold*: holds are inventory, not money; the inventory port has nothing to do with refunds.

excerpts.quote: Refunds are bounded by the unrefunded captured amount and delegated to an idempotent provider.

notes.title: Failing merchant webhooks back off, then dead-letter
notes.body:
Merchant webhooks are at-least-once. Per ADR-0011, a failed delivery **retries with exponential backoff and moves to a dead-letter queue after six total attempts**; every request carries a stable delivery ID, and consumers deduplicate by that ID. `MerchantWebhookWorker` matches the ADR: on failure it dead-letters once `attempt` reaches 5 (the sixth try) and otherwise schedules a retry after `1000 * 2 ** attempt` ms.

- *Every minute for an hour, then dropped*: the delay doubles, and failures land in a dead-letter queue rather than vanishing.
- *Three quick retries, then suspension*: the cap is six attempts with growing delays, and nothing suspends the merchant.
- *Retry forever, dedupe by order ID*: retries are bounded, and dedupe uses the delivery ID.

excerpts.quote: Failures retry with exponential backoff and move to a dead-letter queue after six total attempts.
if (delivery.attempt >= 5) {

notes.title: The buyer is charged the exact quote they saw
notes.body:
ADR-0012 builds a buyer-currency quote from a **dated** rational exchange rate, rounds it **once**, displays it through `Intl.NumberFormat`, and sends **the exact same minor-unit integer and currency** to the payment provider. It forbids silently displaying a conversion while charging the base currency, and every quote records when its rate applied, so buyers pay the number they saw.

- *Charge the base amount and let the provider convert*: that is the forbidden case; the provider's rate would differ from the displayed one.
- *Re-quote at the latest rate when charging*: the quote is dated and fixed; a new rate would change the price after the buyer saw it.
- *Parse the display string back*: the integer is sent directly; formatted text is only for display.

excerpts.quote: send the exact same minor-unit integer and currency to the payment provider.
Buyers pay the number they saw and every quote records when its FX rate applied.

notes.title: What switches on the waiting room
notes.body:
The capacity plan scales stateless tiers automatically and pre-scales the database for announced events, because stateful capacity arrives slowly. For a sudden flash spike it does two things: rate-limit automation first, and **activate a signed waiting room when checkout p95 exceeds 500 ms or DB lock wait exceeds 100 ms for five minutes**. Both signals measure the stateful checkout path, which is what the room protects.

- *Checkout p95 over 2 s or database CPU*: the plan's checkout threshold is 500 ms, and CPU is not a named trigger.
- *An error spike for one minute*: the plan uses a sustained five-minute window on latency and lock wait.
- *Queue depth or worker memory*: queue age drives worker autoscaling, not the waiting room.

excerpts.quote: activate a signed waiting room when checkout p95 exceeds 500 ms or DB lock wait exceeds 100 ms for five minutes.
